concept.name: Conversion
concept.definition: A conversion is an arbitrage position consisting of long the underlying, long a put, and short a call at the same strike and expiration — long stock plus a synthetic short stock via options, per the CFTC glossary definition. The legs offset into a near-riskless position whose value at expiration equals the strike, so it is traded when the combined price deviates from put-call parity fair value.
concept.intuition: You hold the stock and simultaneously hold its exact mirror image built from options; the two cancel, and any small pricing mismatch between them is the arbitrage profit.
concept.mechanics: Long stock + long put + short call (same K, same expiry) has a constant expiration value of K, independent of the underlying's path. The position is established when the synthetic short (short call + long put) is rich relative to actual stock; profit is the locked-in deviation, financed at prevailing rates until expiration.
concept.formula: Expiration value = S_T + max(K - S_T, 0) - max(S_T - K, 0) = K; fair setup cost approximates PV(K) by put-call parity.
concept.failure_modes: The 'riskless' label ignores execution: legging risk, borrow/assignment on the short call before ex-dividend dates (which strips the stock and breaks the hedge), and financing-cost changes can exceed the thin arbitrage margin. Pin risk at expiration adds uncertainty about residual positions.
concept.misconceptions: Conversions are not free money available to retail: in liquid markets the parity deviation is usually smaller than transaction costs, and early-assignment events turn a flat position into a directional one.
concept.example: Buy 100 XYZ shares at $100, buy the $100 put for $4.00, sell the $100 call for $4.60: net cost $99.40 for a position that will be worth exactly $100 at expiration, locking in $0.60 before carry costs.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
